# AGENTS.md — venira-mcp (standalone MCP server)

Repo-specific notes for coding agents. `README.md` (user docs) and `CONTRIBUTING.md` (release
process) are loaded too; this file only holds what is slow to re-derive.

## How to work in this repo

This is the MCP server the other agents talk to; an edit that breaks its contract, breaks every
client. Follow the same loop the skills teach, scoped to the server itself:

1. **Orient** — `recent_files` for what moved; `list_files`/`search` for
   exact layout. In unfamiliar territory call `plan_read_batch` and run its suggestion
   (`read_batch`, max 8 files per call).
2. **Checkpoint** — `snapshot action=create` with a narrow `paths` set and a descriptive
   label before touching behavior, config, or more than one file. Git is the floor, snapshots
   are the ceiling.
3. **Edit** — smallest change that fixes the problem; no drive-by cleanups. Prefer
   `edit_file` (exact `old_text`, `expected_sha256` on re-reads); `apply_patch` /
   `edit_batch` for a multi-file change that cannot land half-written. Routine git
   (`add`, `commit`, `merge`, `rebase`, plain `push`) runs without approval; force / delete /
   URL pushes do not — see `README.md` § Approvals.
4. **Verify** — read the diff (`git_diff`), build if you compiled anything
   (`npm run build`), then the narrowest check first: `npm run test:<suite>`. Full gate =
   `npm run verify` (must be green) plus `npm run doctor` on host-sensitive changes. If a check
   fails, read the log first and only then edit; do not retry the identical command blindly.

## Shape of the repo

- One npm package, no monorepo. `server.ts` = MCP entrypoint (stdio transport + the model-facing
  `INSTRUCTIONS` block). `lib/` = backend implementation. `tools/` = MCP tool layer.
  `scripts/` = test/bench/release scripts. `dist/` = build output (git-ignored).
- Request path: `tools/project.ts` wires everything; tool groups register in
  `tools/project-register-{files,shell,ops,codeintel,workflow,vcs}.ts` → cached executor
  (`tools/project-cache.ts`) → `lib/corehost*.ts`, a **pure-Node** implementation of the
  `project_tool.*` operations (no external binary — the old Rust corehost is gone).
- Envelopes (`ok/kind/data/hint`) are built only via `lib/output.ts` (`buildEnvelope`,
  `errorEnvelope`, `batchEnvelope`); never hand-roll one.
- Tool schemas: shared zod fragments + the `config()` helper live in `tools/project-schema.ts`.
  The model-facing wording for every tool lives in `tools/project-docs.ts` (`TOOL_DOCS`).
- Shell command classification (allow/ask/deny) lives in `lib/shell-policy*.ts` — many small
  modules, one per rule family (`shell-policy-tables.ts` is the rule tables).
- Local git is a first-class capability (`tools/project-git*` + `lib/git-local*.ts`): status,
  diff, log, blame, branch, commit, stash. Read-only git runs free; plain push is allowed;
  everything else with an effect still respects the shell policy.
- Routines are cache-aware: write/move/apply/edit invalidate the whole cache; list/search are
  TTL-cached. `recent_files`, `read_batch` etc. are served warm; distorted
  behaviour usually means the binary changed but the running server did not — re-ask or
  restart the client.

## Commands

```
npm ci                     # better-sqlite3 is native: prebuild, else `npm rebuild better-sqlite3`
npm run build              # tsc -> dist/  (REQUIRED before verify/doctor; see below)
npx tsc --noEmit           # type-check only
npm run check:source-shape # no file in lib/scripts/tools may be a single line >2 KB
npm run check:docs         # README/tool-count/version/env-doc gate (first step of `verify`)
npm run verify             # behavioural suite (many focused scripts + scripts/verify.ts)
npm run smoke              # in-process sanity check
npm run doctor             # preflight: workspace, data dir, ripgrep, tool count, health, shell
npm run bench:mcp          # end-to-end numbers for PRs
```

- **`npm run build` first.** `scripts/verify.ts` and `scripts/doctor.ts` launch `node dist/server.js`,
  so they test the *build*, not your source. `npm run verify` does not build for you.
- Single suites: `npm run test:<name>` — current list in `package.json` under `scripts`.
  `test:shell-*`, `test:balanced-read-only`, `test:restore-checkpoint`, `test:audit-fallback`
  are **not** in the `verify` chain; run them by hand when the area changes.
- CI order (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`): build → `tsc --noEmit` → `check:source-shape` → smoke →
  doctor → verify → `test:policy-corpus` → `bench:mcp`. Matrix: ubuntu/windows/macOS × Node 20/22/24.
- `npm run coverage:shell` needs Node >= 22.8 (the coverage flags do not exist on Node 20);
  it skips the floors on older Node instead of failing.

## Contracts that break CI when broken

- **New or renamed tool** — four places, all enforced:
  1. register it in the right `tools/project-register-*.ts` using `config()` from
     `tools/project-schema.ts`;
  2. add a `TOOL_DOCS` entry in `tools/project-docs.ts` (`test:tool-schema` fails otherwise);
  3. record its `tools/list` size in `scripts/schema-budget.json`
     (`npm run test:schema-budget -- --update --allow-increase`; a tool with no recorded
     ceiling fails the check, and ceilings otherwise only ratchet **down**);
  4. tool counts changed → update the README count strings **and**
     `scripts/check-docs.ts` (`EXPECTED_DEFAULT_TOOLS` / `EXPECTED_EXPERT_TOOLS`) together.
     README says 39 default / 52 expert; `schema-budget.json` records the same
     counts (52 expert / 39 default) with `execute_js` registered.
- **Version bump** — `package.json`, `package-lock.json` (both `version` and `packages[""].version`),
  `server.json` (both `version` and `packages[]`) and `lib/version.ts` must all agree;
  `check:docs` fails otherwise.
- **New `VENIRA_*` variable** — add it to `ENV_REGISTRY` in `lib/env-registry.ts`
  (`test:env-registry` compares the registry against the runtime source) *and* to the README
  env table (`check:docs` compares the docs against the source).
- Every boolean tool flag is the integer `0|1` (`flag01` in `tools/project-schema.ts`), every
  parameter needs a non-empty description, and `reason` (max 400 chars) is audit-logged on
  mutating calls.
- Shell policy changes need `npm run test:policy-corpus` (corpus: `scripts/policy-corpus.json`
  + `scripts/policy-corpus-extra.ts`) — the corpus pins tier **and** rule id per command.

## Quirks

- ESM + TypeScript strict: relative imports end in `.js` even though the source is `.ts`.
  `tsconfig` has `rootDir: "."`, so `dist/` mirrors the tree (`dist/lib/…`, `dist/scripts/…`).
- Any script under `scripts/` that touches `VENIRA_*` must `import "./clean-env.js"` **first** —
  inherited `VENIRA_*` vars from the launching agent session leak in and cause false failures.
- zod v4 (`z.looseObject`, `.meta()`); `tools/list` serves zod's JSON Schema, which is what
  the schema-budget script measures.
- `lib/output.ts` reads `VENIRA_OUTPUT_MODE` at module load — env changes need a restart.
- Node >= 20 (`engines`); CI covers 20/22/24.
- Git-ignored local-only files — do not treat as canonical and do not commit:
  `.mcp.json`, `mcp.json`, `Bug.txt`, `ROADMAP*.md`, `PUSH-NOTES.md`, `docs/`, `set-secret.js`,
  `wait-ci.js`.
- `G:\Venira\Venira-mcp-skills\` (outside this repo) holds the Claude-skills versions of the
  workflows in this file (`venira-coding-workflow`, `venira-add-tool`, `venira-debug-ci`,
  `venira-git-pr`). If you are asked to follow those skills, prefer the exact text there —
  this file is deliberately a compact index, not a copy.
- Commits follow conventional commits (`feat(scope):`, `fix(scope):`, `chore(release):`).
  A release = bump the version in the four places above, then
  `npm run build && npm run check:docs && npm run check:source-shape && npm run verify`,
  then tag `v<x.y.z>` (tag push triggers `.github/workflows/release.yml`).

## Working on this repo with the Venira MCP tools

The repo's own client config (`.mcp.json`, local only) runs `dist/server.js`, so **rebuild after
source edits** or the MCP tools serve the old build.

- Start with `recent_files` (limit 10–20) instead of guessing files; feed the paths
  into `read_batch` (max 8 items). `plan_read_batch` returns a ready batch call
  for an unfamiliar area.
- 2+ reads → one `read_batch`. One file → `read_file` with `start_line/end_line`
  or `ranges[]` (max 16); follow `next_start_line` when truncated.
- Prefer `edit_file` (exact `old_text`→`new_text`, `expected_sha256` for a verified
  re-read) over `write_file`; `edit_batch` for multi-file, all-or-nothing edits.
- Take a `snapshot` before multi-file/overwrite/delete work. Restore with
  `dry_run=1` first, then `verify=1, delete_extra=0`; never `delete_extra=1`.
- Pass `reason` ("why", <=400 chars) on every write/edit/delete/snapshot/PR/CI call — it lands in
  the audit trail.
- `shell_run` returns `run_id`; poll `shell_status` until `running=false`, or use
  `background: 0` for short commands whose output you need now. `ok=true` only means the call
  completed — read `command_status`/`exit_code`.
- `approval_required`: stop, show the user `approval_id` and `approve_command`, retry once after
  they confirm. Never approve it yourself and never loop.
- Treat `ok:false` + `retryable:false` as final; follow the envelope's `hint`/`next_actions`.

# Add a tool to the Venira MCP server

New tools must look and behave like the existing ones, because clients and agents rely on consistent descriptions, schemas, and error shapes. Learn the conventions from the code, then copy them.

## 1. Learn the conventions first

- `recent_files` and `list_files` on the `tools/`, `lib/`, and `scripts/verify/` folders.
- Read one or two tools close to the new one (for example a small read-only tool and a mutating one) with `read_batch`.
- Find where tools are registered: `search` (kind `literal_content`) for an existing tool name, and follow it to the registry.
- Note the helpers the existing tools share: workspace path validation, error codes, audit logging, output-mode trimming.

## 2. Design the tool

- Name: `project_<verb>_<noun>`, consistent with neighbours.
- Description: follow the house style seen in existing tools: one line of what it does, then `Use when:`, `Avoid when:`, and `Output:`.
- Input schema: bounded numbers (min/max), `0/1` flags the way existing tools do them, and an optional `reason` for the audit log if the tool mutates anything.
- Decide read-only vs mutating up front. Mutating tools need path safety and snapshot or rollback advice in their description.

## 3. Implement

Checkpoint first with `snapshot` (include the registry file, README, and CHANGELOG in `paths`). Then create the tool file with `write_file` (`mode=create`) and register it with `edit_file`. Reuse shared helpers instead of re-implementing path checks or error handling.

## 4. Verify

- Add a case to the matching script under `scripts/verify/` (or a dedicated test script) covering success, a not-found or invalid input, and any size limits.
- Run the type-check/build and the verify script with `shell_run`. Feed failures to `explain_error`.
- Run the project's doctor or consistency script if one exists, since it often cross-checks the tool list against docs.

## 5. Document

Update the README tool list and add a CHANGELOG entry. Then review everything with `git_diff` and report: tool name, files touched, snapshot id, and which checks passed.

# Venira coding workflow

Venira tools make edits auditable and reversible. Follow this loop so every change is small, checkpointed and verified, and a mistake costs one restore instead of an hour of cleanup.

Clients may prefix tool names (for example `mcp__venira__read_file`). The tool name (without the server prefix) is the stable name.

## Ground rules

- Stay inside the workspace. Paths are workspace-relative; forward slashes work on Windows too.
- Read before you write. Never edit from memory of a file. Re-read when anything else may have touched it.
- Make the smallest change that solves the task. No drive-by reformatting or unrelated cleanups.
- Never put secrets in files, commands or chat. Store tokens with `secret` (prefer `value_env`) and inject them with `secret_env` on `shell_run`.
- Delete, overwrite, move-over and destructive git operations only when the user asked, and only after a snapshot.
- If intent is ambiguous and the change is hard to undo, ask one short question. Otherwise proceed and state your assumptions in the report.

## 1. Orient

- `recent_files` (depth 2-3, limit 20-30) shows what moved lately and which files are in play.
- In an unfamiliar area, `plan_read_batch` with a one-line task description, then run the `read_batch` it proposes (max 8 files per call).
- For big files use `outline_symbol` first, then `read_file` with `start_line`/`end_line` or `ranges`.
- Never guess paths. Use `search` (`file_name`, `literal_content`, `definition`) or `list_files`.
- Read project instructions if they exist (AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, README) before the first edit.

## 2. Checkpoint

Create a snapshot (`snapshot`, `action=create`, narrow `paths`, label like `before <what>`) before edits that span several files, deletes, moves or overwrites of anything git does not hold, and large refactors. Skip it for a tiny single-file edit already covered by git. Check `truncated` and `skipped` in the result, and keep the snapshot id for the report and for any rollback (see §5).

## 3. Edit

| Need | Tool |
|---|---|
| One targeted change | `edit_file` with exact `old_text`, plus `expected_sha256`; use `edits[]` for several replacements in one file |
| Several files that must land together | `edit_batch` (all-or-nothing, automatic rollback) |
| Change that arrives as a diff | `apply_patch`, `dry_run=1` first |
| New file | `write_file` `mode=create`, `create_dirs=1` |
| Replace a whole file | `write_file` `mode=overwrite` with `expected_sha256`, after a snapshot |
| Rename or move | `move_path` (not undoable, snapshot first) |
| Duplicate | `copy_path` |
| Delete | `delete_path` (`recursive=1` for folders), only on request, snapshot first |

Before changing a shared symbol, signature or file name, run `change_impact` (pass `symbols` or `files`) to list dependents and the tests affected. Pass a short `reason` on mutating calls so the audit trail explains why.

## 4. Verify

- Review the change with `git_diff` (`include_patch=1`) or `diff_files`.
- Run the narrowest check first (type-check or one test), then the full suite once before finishing. Use `shell_run` with `background=0` for short commands. For long ones use `background=1`, then `shell_status` with `wait_seconds` until `running=false`.
- Pick the shell explicitly when syntax matters. Windows PowerShell 5.1 has no `&&`: chain with `;`, or use `pwsh` or `bash`.
- On failure, pass the stderr to `explain_error`, confirm the cause in the code, then fix. Do not retry blindly.
- Fix and re-verify until clean. If you cannot run a check, say so instead of implying it passed.

## 5. Roll back

`snapshot` `action=restore` with the id: first `dry_run=1` to preview, then `verify=1`. Use `paths` to restore only some files. Use `delete_extra=1` only when you really want files created after the snapshot removed. Restore beats hand-reverting because it is exact.

## Error recovery

| Signal | Meaning | Do this |
|---|---|---|
| `not_found` | Wrong path | `search` for the name. Do not guess. |
| `old_text_not_found` | File changed, or whitespace or line endings differ | Read `data.mismatch` and `data.context`, re-read that range, retry with exact text |
| `old_text_ambiguous` | Text matches several places | Widen `old_text` with surrounding lines. `replace_all=1` only if every match should change |
| `expected_sha256` refused | File changed since you read it | Re-read, re-apply the change. Never force it |
| `conflict` | Target already exists | Choose another path, or snapshot then `overwrite` if intended |
| `batch_failed` | Everything was rolled back (`rollback_succeeded`) | Fix the item named in `data.executed` and `data.skipped`, rerun the batch |
| `approval_required` | A human must approve | Tell the user, give `data.approval.approve_command` or use `approval_wait_s`, retry once with `approval_id`. Do not work around it |
| `repeated_failure` | The identical command already failed | Read `data.previous.stderr_tail` and change the command. `retry_failed=1` only for flaky or environmental failures |
| `truncated: true` | Output was cut | Continue with `start_line=next_start_line`, or narrow `relative_path`, `limit` or `depth` |
| Odd or stale results | Cache out of sync after external changes | `cache_clear`, then `health` (sections `warnings`, `posture`) |

Keep it short and factual: files changed, snapshot id (if any), checks run and their result, and anything left undone or assumed.

# Debug builds and CI with Venira

Find the root cause from evidence (logs, error text), fix it, and prove the fix. Retrying without reading the log wastes CI minutes and hides real problems.

## 1. Get the evidence

- Local failure: reproduce with `shell_run` (`background=0` for short commands). Capture the stderr tail.
- CI failure: `ci_status` with `pr`, `branch`, or `ref` to find the failing run. Pass `run_id` to see its jobs, then `ci_logs` with the failing `job_id` (start with the default tail, widen `tail_lines` only if needed).

## 2. Classify the failure

Pass the error block to `explain_error`. It matches known signatures (TypeScript, Python, git, npm, GitHub) offline and returns likely cause plus next actions. Treat that as a hypothesis and confirm it against the code:
- Locate the failing file and line with `search` and `read_file` (ranges).
- If the failure points at a changed symbol, check `change_impact`.
- Separate three causes: a code bug, a flaky or environment problem (timeouts, network, cache), and a config or dependency drift. Each has a different fix.

## 3. Fix

Follow the venira-coding-workflow habits: snapshot if the fix is multi-file, edit surgically, then re-run the exact failing command locally. If `shell_run` answers `repeated_failure`, read `data.previous.stderr_tail` and change the approach instead of passing `retry_failed=1`.

## 4. Confirm on CI

- Push (via `shell_run`, e.g. `git push`), then `ci_wait` on the branch or PR. If `terminal=false`, call again with the same selector.
- Use `ci_control` with `retry_failed` only for confirmed flaky jobs, and always give a `reason`.
- Use `ci_trigger` only when a workflow supports manual dispatch or no new commit is available.

## Report

State the root cause in one or two sentences, the fix, and the evidence that it works (local command result and CI overall status). If it was flaky or environmental, say so plainly rather than claiming a code fix.

# venira-mcp

Fast, workspace-scoped MCP server for coding agents (OpenCode, Claude Desktop, any MCP client).
Three tool modes — **Core** (23 tools: shell, `execute_js`, read/search/list, edit/create/move, snapshot, git, memory — for small models) · **Default** (39 coding tools + shell, no CI/CD) · **Expert** (52 tools: default + CI/CD). `VENIRA_JS_EXEC_MODE=off` hides `execute_js` in every mode (52 → 51, 39 → 38, 23 → 22); otherwise it is registered and approval-gated. `VENIRA_SETUP_TOOLS=1` adds the two setup tools `detect_harnesses` and `install_self` (+2); `npx venira-mcp --install` and `--print-config` do the same from a terminal.
Pure Node, 1 native dependency (better-sqlite3), no GUI, no external binary.

> **Security scope.** Venira is a guard rail with an audit trail, not a sandbox. It runs with the privileges of the OS user that started it. The workspace lock limits the paths the file tools can touch (unless `VENIRA_UNRESTRICTED=1`), not what a shell command does: commands are classified by rules (allow / ask / deny) and every call is audited, but a malicious prompt can still steer the agent into running a harmful command that the active profile lets through (with `off`, every command runs). Anything running as the same OS user can read the keys in `VENIRA_DATA_DIR`. For untrusted workspaces, or whenever you need a real isolation boundary, run Venira in a container or VM. Details: [`SECURITY.md`](./SECURITY.md).

## 1. Setup

**One-line install** (run in your project, then restart the client):

```bash
npx --yes venira-mcp@latest --install auto --workspace .
```

Prefer your agent? Paste this prompt into OpenCode/Claude/Cursor:

```text
Set up Venira MCP for this workspace.
1. Detect my MCP client config path.
2. Run: npx --yes venira-mcp@latest --install auto --workspace .
3. Restart the client. Then call health to verify.
```

**Manual config** (pick your client):

| Client | Config path | Format |
|---|---|---|
| VS Code | `<workspace>/.vscode/mcp.json` | JSONC |
| OpenCode | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.jsonc` | JSONC |
| Claude Desktop | `claude_desktop_config.json` | JSON |
| Cursor | `~/.cursor/mcp.json` | JSON |
| Codex | `~/.codex/config.toml` | TOML |

All use the same `npx` command. See §2 for ready-to-copy JSON/TOML.

In this repo `.vscode/mcp.json` is git-ignored because it holds machine-specific settings (and may relax security flags). Copy `.vscode/mcp.example.json` to `.vscode/mcp.json` and adjust it locally.
## 2. Client configs (copy-paste)

The examples use two environment variables: the workspace and the tool set. Everything else has a safe default, so you only add a `VENIRA_*` variable when you want to change that default (see [Config recipes](#config-recipes)).

**OpenCode / VS Code / Cursor / Claude / Kimi / DeepSeek / Antigravity** — use the wrapper format supported by your client:

        // Small model / restricted context? Uncomment to slim tools/list:

### Config recipes

Pick one block and put its variables in the `env` section of your client config. Every other variable keeps its default.

| Recipe | Variables |
|---|---|
| Minimal (recommended) | `VENIRA_WORKSPACE`, `VENIRA_TOOL_MODE=expert` |
| Fewer prompts on a personal machine | Minimal, plus `VENIRA_SECURITY_PROFILE=trusted` |
| Full trust (isolated or personal machine only) | Minimal, plus `VENIRA_SECURITY_PROFILE=off` |

`off` keeps full trust: shell checks off (hard-deny included), no workspace lock (`VENIRA_UNRESTRICTED=1`), `VENIRA_JS_EXEC_MODE=auto` as the default JS mode, no elicitation, full env passed to shell, `reveal=true` prints secrets and nothing prompts. A variable you set yourself always wins over the profile (e.g. `VENIRA_JS_EXEC_MODE=off` stays `off`). Deliberate opt-ins are never implied: `VENIRA_SHELL_OVERRIDES`, `VENIRA_ALLOW_SELF_INSTALL` and `VENIRA_SECRET_KEYCHAIN`.

Do not write a variable just to restate its default (for example `VENIRA_OUTPUT_MODE=full`, `VENIRA_USE_RIPGREP=1` or `VENIRA_SECURITY_PROFILE=balanced`).

### Security profiles

| `VENIRA_SECURITY_PROFILE` | Shell policy | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `strict` | `strict` | Read-only and workspace-local allowlist runs without approval |
| `balanced` (default) | `balanced` | Recommended general-purpose setting |
| `trusted` | `permissive` | Ask-rule and unclassified commands run; hard-deny commands require approval |
| `off` | `off` | Full trust: shell checks off, no workspace lock, JS exec `auto`, no elicitation, full env passed to shell. Prints a warning and audits shell commands. Replaces setting those variables one by one; any of them you set explicitly still wins |

`VENIRA_SHELL_MODE` is an advanced override and takes precedence over the profile. `VENIRA_JS_EXEC_MODE` separately gates the JavaScript tool: `off` (default) hides it, `ask` registers it with per-call human approval (skipped when `VENIRA_PERMISSION_MODE=allow_all`), `semi-auto` registers it without approval but keeps the containment (workspace-only fs, scrubbed env, no child processes; network is always open), `auto` registers it without approval and without any containment (full fs access, inherited env; personal machines only). `switch_workspace` follows the profile the same way: `trusted`/`off` (and an explicit `VENIRA_UNRESTRICTED=1`) switch to any existing directory; `strict`/`balanced` switch only inside `VENIRA_WORKSPACE_ROOTS`, which unset locks switching to the spawn workspace.

> Choose `trusted` when you want fewer prompts on a personal machine. Choose `off` only when you intentionally accept that shell checks are disabled; JS exec is still gated by `VENIRA_JS_EXEC_MODE` (a human gate for `execute_js` only counts when that mode is `ask` and `VENIRA_PERMISSION_MODE` is not `allow_all`). The `secret_env` gate remains active in every profile. Elicitation hangs off the shell mode: `strict` never prompts (CLI grant only), `balanced` prompts for every unclassified ask-rule command, `permissive` never prompts at all (only the `command_substitution` always-ask rule, hard-deny commands downgraded to `ask.deny.*`, and `secret_env` still prompt), `off` never prompts.

### Advanced configuration

| Variable | Default | Change when |
|---|---|---|
| `VENIRA_SHELL_MODE` | Profile mapping | You need to override only the shell policy (`strict`, `balanced`, `permissive`, or `off`) |
| `VENIRA_JS_EXEC_MODE` | `off` | `ask` registers `execute_js` with per-call approval (skipped when `VENIRA_PERMISSION_MODE=allow_all`); `semi-auto` registers it without approval but contained; `auto` registers it without approval and without containment |
| `VENIRA_UNRESTRICTED` | `0` | Keep workspace path restrictions enabled; do not set to `1` in production |

See the full environment reference in §6 for caching, shell, provider, and diagnostic options.

## 3. Benchmark (per-op, p50)

Measured: Windows + Node 24, standalone build, 2026-11-01.

| Op | p50 | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Cached `read_file` | 8.0 ms | warm cache |
| `read_file` (multi, 8 files) | 12.8 ms | one call, 8 items |
| `get_file_info` | 6.2 ms | cached |
| `search` (literal, `*.ts`) | 11.5 ms | p95 ≈ 1.3 s (file count dependent) |
| `health` (no DB) | 28.5 ms | |
| `shell_run` + status | ~930 ms | 2 s wait budget dominates |
| **First call** | **113.7 ms** | post warm-up |

> Batch: 8 reads as one batch call (16.6 ms) vs 8× individual (~76 ms) — the round-trip saving
> that makes the agent loop fast.

### Agent tool-path benchmark: Venira MCP vs Codex `exec_command`

Measured on 2026-11-07 on one Windows 11 build 26200 machine (Intel Core i5-1035G1,
8 logical processors, 11.8 GiB RAM, Node v24.20.0). Each workload used 20 paired
samples per phase, alternating call order. Venira used the persistent MCP connection;
each native `exec_command` call launched a fresh PowerShell process. Cache-miss samples
cleared Venira's in-process cache; warm samples reused it. The OS filesystem cache stayed
warm.

| Workload | Phase | Venira p50 / p95 | `exec_command` p50 / p95 | Ratio of p50s |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Read first lines of 8 files in one batch | Cache miss | 53.5 / 72 ms | 962 / 1,121 ms | 17.98× |
| Read first lines of 8 files in one batch | Warm | 39 / 60 ms | 1,103.5 / 1,549 ms | 28.29× |
| Search `VENIRA_WORKSPACE` across the workspace (49 hits) | Cache miss | 118.5 / 188 ms | 1,034.5 / 1,507 ms | 8.73× |

## 4. Three tool modes

Three tool modes set which tools the client sees. Set via `VENIRA_TOOL_MODE` env var or
`"toolMode"` in `venira.config.json` (env wins). `VENIRA_DISABLE_TOOLS` hides additional tools on top.
`core` is the small-model / restricted-context preset (the old `VENIRA_PROFILE=core`, now folded into this one variable). Unlike the other two modes it is an **allowlist**: only the must-have tools below are advertised, and any tool added later stays out of `tools/list` until it is added to `CORE_TOOLS` (`tools/project-tool-mode.ts`), because every extra schema costs tokens on every prompt.

| Mode | Tools | Includes |
|---|---|---|
| `core` | **22** | Allowlist: `shell_run`, `shell_status`, `shell_cancel`, `execute_js`, `read_file`, `search`, `list_files`, `recent_files`, `outline_symbol`, `edit_file` (single **and** multi-file via `edits[]` with per-item `relative_path`, or `requests[]` on `read_file`), `write_file`, `delete_path`, `create`, `move_path`, `snapshot`, `git_status`, `git_diff`, `git_log`, `git_branch`, `git_commit`, `git_stash`, `memory` |
| `default` | **37** | Read/write/edit/search, code intel, snapshots, shell, `delete_path`, `execute_js` — **no** CI/CD; `explain_error` and `plan_read_batch` are expert-only |
| `expert` | **50** | Everything in default + `pr_*`, `ci_*`, `explain_error`, `plan_read_batch` |

- Order is blobs, then indexes, then `project.json`, so the mirror never holds a checkpoint whose blobs are missing. Every copy is verified (blob sha256 equals its file name; index bytes equal the source) before it gets its final name. A corrupt local blob blocks only the checkpoints that use it.
- Append-only: venira never deletes anything at the mirror. A checkpoint pruned locally (`VENIRA_SNAPSHOT_KEEP`) or deleted stays at the mirror until you remove it by hand, so expect it to grow; the only overwrite is `verify=true` replacing a file that no longer matches its source.
- Bounded: a run stops between files once its time budget is spent and reports `partial` / `timed_out`; run it again to resume (only missing files are copied). A first sync of a large store may need a few runs.

## 8. Envelopes & error codes

Success:

```jsonc
{ "ok": true, "status": "completed", "kind": "file_read", "data": { … }, "hint": "Next chunk: …", "elapsed_ms": 2.57 }
```

Failure:

```jsonc
{ "ok": false, "status": "failed", "error": { "code": "not_found", "message": "…", "retryable": false }, "hint": "Check with list_files first", "next_actions": [{ "tool": "list_files", "arguments": { "relative_path": "." } }] }
```

`ok` describes the tool operation. For `shell_run`, a command that ran and exited non-zero still has `ok: true`, but the envelope `status` names the command: `completed`, `failed`, `running`, `cancelled` (or `unknown` when the shell never reported an exit code). `command_status` repeats the same outcome in the shell vocabulary (`succeeded` / `failed` / `running` / `cancelled`) and `hint` says what to do next. A read batch with failed items reports top-level `ok: false`, `status: "partial"`, and `error.code: "batch_partial_failure"`; inspect `data.responses` for each result.

**Timestamps and ordering.** Every timestamp a tool reports is epoch **milliseconds** and says so in its field name (`started_at_ms`, `completed_at_ms`, `created_at_ms`, `timestamp_ms`); the only exception is the `since_unix` filter of `read_audit`, which takes seconds. Every "recent list" reads **newest first**: the audit rows, the checkpoints and the trace buffer.

**Counts vs. caps.** A tool that caps a list says so: `count` is what was found, `returned` is what came back, `omitted` is what the cap cut, and `limited: true` marks the cut (`symbol_references`, `search`, `list_files`).

In `compact` mode, shortened payloads set `trimmed: true` and `truncated: true`; `summary` describes omitted content. For an otherwise unsupported large payload, `data.preview_text` contains a bounded JSON-text preview and `summary` reports the original size and shape. Large error messages or attached error data are also explicitly marked as trimmed. Use `full` when the complete payload is required.

Common codes: `not_found`, `invalid_request`, `old_text_not_found`, `old_text_ambiguous`, `stale_content`, `repeated_failure`, `command_denied`, `shell_unavailable`, `path_escape`, `resource_limit`, `sensitive_result`, `unsupported`, `internal`.

## 9. Agent instructions (paste into `AGENTS.md` / `CLAUDE.md`)

```text
Venira MCP rules:
1. Unfamiliar task: call plan_read_batch first, then run steps[0].
2. Read with `read_file` — `relative_path` for a single file, or `requests[]` (max 8) to read several files in one call. Never re-read a file a tool already returned.
3. Prefer edit_file over write_file; pass `reason` on every mutation.
4. Snapshot before multi-file or destructive changes.
5. Short commands: shell_run with background: false. Long jobs: background: true, then poll shell_status.
6. Do not call execute_js unless the user asked for JS; in `ask` mode it needs per-call approval. Network access is always open in every mode; in `semi-auto` the filesystem is limited to the workspace and the environment is scrubbed, in `auto` the containment is dropped.
7. On failure, follow the envelope's hint. Treat ok:false + retryable:false as final.
8. Report only what the tool returned.
9. On [approval_required]: stop, tell the user the approval_id and approve_command, do not loop or approve it yourself; retry once with data.approval.retry_with after they confirm. Use dry_run: true to preview a command's tier.
```

## What these numbers mean

The live comparison measures practical tool-path latency: a persistent MCP connection versus a new PowerShell process for every Codex `exec_command`. It does not measure raw filesystem speed in isolation. The component benchmark shows that native PowerShell is faster for uncached single reads, batch reads and metadata; Venira is faster for uncached listing and search and on every warm row. The live comparison above was measured on Venira 1.15.1 and was not re-run on 1.17.0 (it needs the Codex `exec_command` tool); the 1.17.0 component numbers are in line with it. The live p95 is based on only 20 samples and is rough. This is one Windows machine and one run, not a cross-platform guarantee.

## 0. Methodology & caveats

- **Single machine/environment.** Sections 1–2 use one host (Windows 11 / NVMe / Node 24). Latency reflects that disk/CPU; treat deltas vs a new baseline, not absolute targets.
- **Foreground shell includes process startup.** `shell_run` (background=0) spawns a child process and waits for exit, so `shell_foreground_ms` includes shell spawn + stdio handshake. Pure tool latency is better read from the in-process `npm run bench` row or from cached reads.
- **Warm-up required.** The first 3 `read_file` warm-ups attach the session cache; the reported "First call" row is post-warm-up. Cold runs (capability open) take ~100-200ms longer.
- **Cache state matters.** Cached-read rows only apply after the warm-up calls; reset with `cache_clear` or a fresh session before re-benchmarking.
- **p95 is only shown when n ≥ 30.** With n=3 or n=10 the p95 mostly restates the observed maximum, so it is omitted for those rows. Use `avg`/`max` for small samples instead.
- Results can be **truncated** (`complete:false` / `truncated:true`) when a limit is hit; check those flags before trusting a number.

## 5. Venira MCP vs native command proxy

Run `npm run bench:tools` (default 100 samples per phase) or
`npm run bench:tools -- --runs=200`. The runner measures the same fixed read,
batch-read, metadata, directory-list, and literal-search requests through a
local MCP stdio client and through PowerShell commands. It reports server time,
MCP end-to-end time, PowerShell operation time, total PowerShell suite process
time, payload size, and whether the normalized results match. It includes both
Venira cache-miss and warm-cache phases and emits a Markdown table plus raw JSON.
Run a single scenario with, for example,
`npm run bench:tools -- --only=search_literal --runs=3`.

The PowerShell side is a repeatable native-command proxy; it does **not** invoke
Codex's built-in `exec_command` wrapper. One PowerShell process loops through the
native scenarios and reports each operation's timing; its total process time is
reported once for the suite. MCP end-to-end timing includes the local stdio
client. Use actual Codex tool calls when measuring Codex wrapper overhead, and
keep that number separate from the proxy's operation timing. Cache-miss clears
Venira's in-process cache only; the operating-system file cache remains warm.
The runner uses a temporary Venira data directory, disables network access and
JS execution, and performs read-only workspace operations.

PowerShell proxy p50 was similar in both runs (e.g. `read_file` 1.56 ms vs 1.23 ms, `list_files_lib` 4.26 ms vs 2.9 ms), so the machine was not slower during the `v1.17.0` run.

**Finding (before the fix below):** `v1.17.0` was clearly slower on cache-miss file operations (single reads ~3×, `get_file_info` ~6×, `list_files` of a directory ~84×). Search and warm `list_files` are within noise. Warm reads, batch reads and `get_file_info` are 1.3–2.3× slower, but only by 0.4–2.5 ms in absolute terms; this A/B cannot separate that from run-to-run noise.

### Cause and fix

**Cause:** between `176036b` and `4c4b311`, `isProtectedPath` in `lib/workspace.ts` gained a loop over `snapshotProtectedRoots(defaultDataDir(), WORKSPACE)` (new `lib/snapshot-paths.ts`). On every path check this recomputed the checkpoint roots (including a `realpathSync.native` of the workspace for the cache key) and then canonicalised each root with exists/realpath calls, in addition to the existing data-dir canonicalisation. `list_files` checks every directory entry, so it paid this per entry. A micro-benchmark of 2000 `isProtectedPath` calls measured **2.17 ms/call on v1.17.0 vs 0.114 ms/call on v1.16.2** (19×).

**Fix:** `lib/workspace.ts` now resolves the canonical protected roots (data dir + checkpoint roots) once per input set and caches them for 2 s. The cache key includes the data dir, workspace and both snapshot env vars, so changing any of them takes effect immediately; the TTL only bounds staleness if a symlink is created or swapped under one of those folders. The per-path canonicalisation of the checked path is unchanged. After the fix the micro-benchmark gives **0.10 ms/call**, `npm run verify` passes (507 checks), and the post-fix numbers in sections 1, 2 and 5 are back at or below the v1.16.2 level.

Pre-fix v1.17.0 `bench:tools` (MCP p50, cache miss, for the record): read_file 11.11 ms, read_batch_3_files 28.94 ms, get_file_info 11.38 ms, list_files_lib 152.62 ms, search_literal 42.25 ms.

- New tool `memory` (default, core and expert modes; 32/39/52 tools). `action=read` returns the saved note; `action=write` replaces it entirely (overwrite, never append; max 6000 bytes so a read always comes back whole, even in compact output mode).

### Added - `change_impact` `min_confidence` traversal filter
- `min_confidence` (`exact` | `likely` | `possible`, default `likely`) prunes impact edges below the chosen confidence; edges skipped for being name-matching guesses at or above `possible` are counted in `stats.filtered_possible` instead of silently widening the result.

- Search results carry `limited_by` (`file_cap` | `match_cap` | `limit`) instead of a bare `complete=false`, and the count-only mode no longer claims `complete=true` when the file-cap truncation applied.

- Symbols are now extracted after stripping comments, strings, template literals, regex literals and Rust lifetimes; brace-noise no longer skews symbol nesting or hides declarations. ### Fixed - `recent_files` index is checked against the disk
- The recent-files index only knows what Venira tools touched, so deleted or externally-edited files lingered with stale size/mtime. Every index candidate is now stat'ed against disk: missing rows are pruned from the index, surviving rows get the real size/mtime and are ranked by it, and the index only answers the request when at least `limit` rows survive the disk check (otherwise it falls through to the filesystem scan).

### Fixed - audit connection no longer fails on a concurrent writer
- The `better-sqlite3` connection used by the audit store now opens with `busy_timeout = 5000`, so a writer holding the lock can no longer make an audit insert fail immediately with `SQLITE_BUSY`.

# CI/CD

This project has two GitHub Actions workflows under [`.github/workflows/`](./.github/workflows/).
Because the standalone build is **pure Node** (no Rust binary), the pipeline is much
simpler than the original Venira monorepo pipeline.

## 1. `ci.yml` — runs on every push / PR

| Job | Matrix | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `test` | **Ubuntu, Windows, macOS** × Node 20 & 22 | `npm ci` → `npm run build` → strict type-check → `smoke` → `doctor` → `verify` → `bench:mcp` (recorded) |
| `package` | Node 20 | `npm pack --dry-run` — verifies the published tarball is well-formed and shows its size |

Everything runs in standard GitHub runners. No self-hosted runner, no repo
variables, no external binary needed — the whole suite is self-contained.

> **`better-sqlite3` + npm v12.** The native module ships prebuilt binaries
> for the supported Node × platform × arch combinations. `package.json`
> carries an `allowScripts` allowlist (`better-sqlite3`, `esbuild`) that was
> generated with `npm approve-scripts`, so on npm v12 (where dependency
> install scripts are off by default) the `install` script still runs and
> the prebuild downloads. If a combo lacks a prebuild, the `npm ci` step
> compiles from source (needs `python3` + build tools, which all three
> runners already have). The `bin/venira-mcp.js` npx entry also

## 2. `release.yml` — runs on tag push (`v*`) or manual dispatch

Three jobs:

1. **`build`**
   - `npm ci` → `npm run build` → `npm run verify`
   - Produces two artifacts:
     - `venira-mcp-*.tgz` — the npm package (for `npm install`)
     - `venira-mcp-*-standalone.zip` — a drop-in bundle with `dist/`,
       `node_modules/`, docs, and `opencode.example.json` (no `npm install`
       needed)

2. **`docker`** (needs `build`)
   - Builds a multi-arch image (`linux/amd64` + `linux/arm64`) via
     `docker/build-push-action`
   - Pushes to **GitHub Container Registry** at `ghcr.io/<owner>/<repo>`
     with tags: the release tag (e.g. `v1.0.0`), the commit SHA, and
     `latest` (only on the default branch `main`)
   - Uses `gha` cache for faster rebuilds

3. **`release`** (needs `build` + `docker`)
   - Resolves the tag (`v*` from the push event, or the `tag` input on
     manual dispatch)
   - Creates a GitHub Release via `softprops/action-gh-release` with both
     bundles attached
   - **Publishes to npm via OIDC trusted publishing** (see §3)
   - Appends SHA-256 checksums **and the `docker pull` command** to the
     release body

### Prerequisites

- The repository must exist on GitHub (for `ghcr.io` push). For private
  repos, the GHCR image is also private — use `docker login` with a PAT that
  has `packages:read` to pull.
- The `docker` job requires the `packages: write` permission, which is
  already declared in the workflow.
- The `release` job requires `contents: write` + `id-token: write`
  (declared in the workflow). `id-token: write` is what npm's OIDC flow
  exchanges for a short-lived publish credential.

### Manual trigger

From the GitHub UI: **Actions → Release → Run workflow → main**, optionally
passing a `tag` input (e.g. `v1.0.0`). When omitted, the workflow picks the
latest `v*` tag.

## 3. Publishing to npm — OIDC trusted publishing (no long-lived token)

Since 2026-07, npm is deprecating 2FA-bypass granular access tokens (GATs)
for publishing (effective ~2027-01). The recommended replacement is **OIDC
trusted publishing**: the GitHub Actions workflow requests a short-lived JWT
from the `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`id-token: write` permission, npm exchanges it for a
scoped, single-use publish credential. Nothing long-lived is stored in the
repo.

**One-time setup (on the npm side):**

```bash
# As a maintainer of the venira-mcp package:
npm login
npm pkg trust add N0moreher0/Venira-mcp   # register the repo as a trusted publisher
```

Or via the web UI: npmjs.com → your package → **Trusted Publishers** →
*Add publisher* → npm → GitHub → `N0moreher0/Venira-mcp`.

**On the GitHub side:** enable Actions (Settings → Actions → General) and
make sure the repo is not restricted to fork-only.

After that, every successful `v*` tag push auto-publishes — the `release`
job's `npm publish` step picks up the OIDC token automatically. No `NPM_TOKEN`
secret, no 2FA-bypass GAT.

> **First publish** (creating the package on npm) still requires a human
> `npm publish` from a logged-in machine — trusted publishing can only
> publish *existing* packages. So:
>
> ```bash
> cd venira-mcp-standalone
> npm login
> npm publish --access public
> ```
>
> Subsequent releases can all go through the workflow.

After publishing, users can run the MCP server without cloning or installing:

```bash
npx -y venira-mcp              # stdio server
npx -y venira-mcp --doctor     # preflight
npx -y venira-mcp --verify     # behavioural suite
```

# Contributing to venira-mcp

Thanks for contributing. This is a small, fast-moving codebase — keep changes surgical and
add a `verify.ts` check for any new tool.

## Before you start

```bash
git clone <repo-url>
cd venira-mcp
npm install
npm run build
npm run doctor          # preflight: workspace, data dir, audit DB, tools
```

The standalone build is pure Node: no external binary or Rust toolchain is
required. `better-sqlite3` is the only native dependency and ships prebuilt
binaries for the supported Node × OS combinations.

## Development loop

```bash
npm run build        # type-check + emit dist/
npm run smoke        # 30 s: corehost reachable, path lock enforced
npm run verify       # a few minutes: behavioural regression (cache, batch, shell, audit, output modes)
npm run bench:mcp    # numbers for PR descriptions
```

Run `verify` after **every** commit. It covers envelope shape, cache invalidation, batch budgets,
search-cache asymmetry, shell run/poll/cancel, audit rows (including `orphan_running` detection),
compact output mode, and tool annotations.

## Code conventions

- **TypeScript strict mode** (`tsconfig.json`). No `any` leaks; `skipLibCheck` is on for SDK types.
- **ESM** (`"type": "module"`). Imports end in `.js` even for `.ts` sources (standard ESM + TS).
- **Zod v4** for tool input schemas. Keep schemas declarative and small.
- **No new runtime dependencies.** The whole point is one `node` + one `zod` + one
  `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`. A new dep needs a strong justification in the PR.
- **Cache invariants** (see [README §7](./README.md#7-security-model) and the cache notes in `lib/`):
  - Reads/info: mtime+size validated.
  - List/search/recent: short TTL, wiped on any mutation.
  - Search with 0 hits: **never cached**.
  - `execute` is serial; `shell_status` and `cancel` are unqueued.
- **Tool descriptions** live in `TOOL_DOCS` (`tools/project-docs.ts`): `applyToolDocs` serves the
  description (`Use when` / `Avoid when` / `Output`) and copies those lines into `_meta.venira`.
  The `config(title, meta, annotations)` helper only carries the machine metadata (`Speed`,
  `Batch-safe`); it takes no description text, so there is nothing to keep in sync.

## Adding a tool

1. Add the registration in `tools/project.ts` → `registerProjectTools`.
2. Route it through `executeCached` if it's read-only; add it to `MUTATING` if it writes.
3. Envelope + hint: use `buildEnvelope` / `errorEnvelope` from `lib/output.ts` — never hand-roll.
4. `scripts/verify/`: add a `check("…", …)` block in the matching section module; update `expectedCount` in that section module (section modules own their counts; `scripts/verify.ts` only orchestrates).
5. `server.ts` → `INSTRUCTIONS` decision tree: one line if it belongs in the flow.
6. `README.md` → tool table + §4 section for the family it belongs to. Tool counts changed? Update `README.md` count strings **and** `scripts/check-docs.ts` (`EXPECTED_DEFAULT_TOOLS` / `EXPECTED_EXPERT_TOOLS`) together in the same commit — `check:docs` fails otherwise (it did, once: run #281). Tool bytes changed? Raise `scripts/verify/core.ts` ceilings and `scripts/schema-budget.json` in the same commit.
7. `npm run build && npm run verify && npm run bench:mcp` — paste bench output in the PR.

## Release process

Checklist, in order. Do not skip the verification steps; they are what keeps the
published artifacts and the public listings honest.

- [ ] Bump `package.json` version **and** `lib/version.ts` (they must match; `verify.ts` checks).
- [ ] `npm run build && npm run check:docs && npm run check:source-shape && npm run verify`.
- [ ] `npm run bench:mcp` and paste the numbers into the release notes.
- [ ] Update `README.md` where behaviour changed (tool counts, env defaults, security
      notes). The README is the source of truth for catalogs that scrape this repo.
- [ ] Commit, tag `v<version>`, push the tag. `release.yml` builds the npm package,
      the standalone zip and the multi-arch GHCR image, then publishes to npm.
- [ ] Verify the published artifacts: `npm view venira-mcp@<version> version`,
      `docker pull ghcr.io/<owner>/<repo>:<version>`.
- [ ] **Public catalog sync** (the step that used to drift):
  1. **Glama** (`glama.ai/mcp/servers`) — the listing is built from the GitHub repo.
     After the tag is public, open the server page and use its refresh action; confirm
     name, description, version, tool list and required env vars match this repo.
     Claim the listing if it is still unowned, so future updates can be pushed.
  2. **Official MCP registry / Smithery** — if the project is listed there, refresh the
     entry from the same release and re-check the install command.
  3. Record the catalog check in the release notes (`Glama: refreshed <date>`), so the
     next release has a visible baseline.
- [ ] Post-release: `health` and `read_audit verify=1` on a fresh
      install; confirm the shell policy profile and protected paths behave as documented.

Changelog lives in the PR / release notes; there is no separate `CHANGELOG.md` (yet).

## Security-sensitive changes

Anything that touches path resolution (`lib/workspace.ts`), the permission model, or shell
execution needs an extra review pass. In particular:

- Never widen `VENIRA_UNRESTRICTED` semantics without discussion.
- New shell options must document what they can do (tail size, timeout, cwd) in the description.
- Audit-row schema changes require a migration note in the PR.

# Venira coding workflow

Venira tools make edits auditable and reversible. Follow this loop so every change is small, checkpointed and verified, and a mistake costs one restore instead of an hour of cleanup.

Clients may prefix tool names (for example `mcp__venira__read_file`). The tool name (without the server prefix) is the stable name.

## Ground rules

- Stay inside the workspace. Paths are workspace-relative; forward slashes work on Windows too.
- Read before you write. Never edit from memory of a file. Re-read when anything else may have touched it.
- Make the smallest change that solves the task. No drive-by reformatting or unrelated cleanups.
- Never put secrets in files, commands or chat. Store tokens with `secret` (prefer `value_env`) and inject them with `secret_env` on `shell_run`.
- Delete, overwrite, move-over and destructive git operations only when the user asked, and only after a snapshot.
- If intent is ambiguous and the change is hard to undo, ask one short question. Otherwise proceed and state your assumptions in the report.

## 1. Orient

- `recent_files` (depth 2-3, limit 20-30) shows what moved lately and which files are in play.
- In an unfamiliar area, `plan_read_batch` with a one-line task description, then run the `read_batch` it proposes (max 8 files per call).
- For big files use `outline_symbol` first, then `read_file` with `start_line`/`end_line` or `ranges`.
- Never guess paths. Use `search` (`file_name`, `literal_content`, `definition`) or `list_files`.
- Read project instructions if they exist (AGENTS.md, CONTRIBUTING.md, README) before the first edit.

## 2. Checkpoint

Create a snapshot (`snapshot`, `action=create`, narrow `paths`, label like `before <what>`) before edits that span several files, deletes, moves or overwrites of anything git does not hold, and large refactors. Skip it for a tiny single-file edit already covered by git. Check `truncated` and `skipped` in the result, and keep the snapshot id for the report and for any rollback (see §5).

## 3. Edit

| Need | Tool |
|---|---|
| One targeted change | `edit_file` with exact `old_text`, plus `expected_sha256`; use `edits[]` for several replacements in one file |
| Several files that must land together | `edit_batch` (all-or-nothing, automatic rollback) |
| Change that arrives as a diff | `apply_patch`, `dry_run=1` first |
| New file | `write_file` `mode=create`, `create_dirs=1` |
| Replace a whole file | `write_file` `mode=overwrite` with `expected_sha256`, after a snapshot |
| Rename or move | `move_path` (not undoable, snapshot first) |
| Duplicate | `copy_path` |
| Delete | `delete_path` (`recursive=1` for folders), only on request, snapshot first |

Before changing a shared symbol, signature or file name, run `change_impact` (pass `symbols` or `files`) to list dependents and the tests affected. Pass a short `reason` on mutating calls so the audit trail explains why.

## 4. Verify

- Review the change with `git_diff` (`include_patch=1`) or `diff_files`.
- Run the narrowest check first (type-check or one test), then the full suite once before finishing. Use `shell_run` with `background=0` for short commands. For long ones use `background=1`, then `shell_status` with `wait_seconds` until `running=false`.
- Pick the shell explicitly when syntax matters. Windows PowerShell 5.1 has no `&&`: chain with `;`, or use `pwsh` or `bash`.
- On failure, pass the stderr to `explain_error`, confirm the cause in the code, then fix. Do not retry blindly.
- Fix and re-verify until clean. If you cannot run a check, say so instead of implying it passed.

## 5. Roll back

`snapshot` `action=restore` with the id: first `dry_run=1` to preview, then `verify=1`. Use `paths` to restore only some files. Use `delete_extra=1` only when you really want files created after the snapshot removed. Restore beats hand-reverting because it is exact.

## Error recovery

| Signal | Meaning | Do this |
|---|---|---|
| `not_found` | Wrong path | `search` for the name. Do not guess. |
| `old_text_not_found` | File changed, or whitespace or line endings differ | Read `data.mismatch` and `data.context`, re-read that range, retry with exact text |
| `old_text_ambiguous` | Text matches several places | Widen `old_text` with surrounding lines. `replace_all=1` only if every match should change |
| `expected_sha256` refused | File changed since you read it | Re-read, re-apply the change. Never force it |
| `conflict` | Target already exists | Choose another path, or snapshot then `overwrite` if intended |
| `batch_failed` | Everything was rolled back (`rollback_succeeded`) | Fix the item named in `data.executed` and `data.skipped`, rerun the batch |
| `approval_required` | A human must approve | Tell the user, give `data.approval.approve_command` or use `approval_wait_s`, retry once with `approval_id`. Do not work around it |
| `repeated_failure` | The identical command already failed | Read `data.previous.stderr_tail` and change the command. `retry_failed=1` only for flaky or environmental failures |
| `truncated: true` | Output was cut | Continue with `start_line=next_start_line`, or narrow `relative_path`, `limit` or `depth` |
| Odd or stale results | Cache out of sync after external changes | `cache_clear`, then `health` (sections `warnings`, `posture`) |

A `trimmed` flag or "Output mode compact" hint only means the payload was shortened. It is not an error.

## Final report

Keep it short and factual: files changed, snapshot id (if any), checks run and their result, and anything left undone or assumed.

# Isolation guides — Docker, WSL, Windows Sandbox

Venira is a **guard rail with an audit trail, not a sandbox**. The workspace lock,
shell policy and protected paths reduce mistakes and make them visible, but they run
with the privileges of the OS user that started the server. When you need a real
isolation boundary — untrusted repository, generated code, an agent you do not fully
trust — run the whole server inside a container or VM, not just the shell commands.

This page covers the three practical options on Windows/Linux, with the mounts,
network controls and limits of each. [`SECURITY.md`](./SECURITY.md) describes the
threat model; [`DOCKER.md`](./DOCKER.md) has the image build details.

## Choosing a boundary

| Option | Isolation strength | Persistence | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Docker container | Strong (namespaces, seccomp, no host FS by default) | Named volumes / bind mounts you choose | Day-to-day untrusted repos; CI-like reproducibility |
| WSL 2 distro | Weak boundary vs. Windows (interop can reach `C:\`, shares the same user) | Full (normal Linux FS) | Linux toolchains; cheap separation, not hostile code |
| Windows Sandbox | Strong (disposable VM, no host FS except mapped folders) | None (destroyed on close) | One-off review of a suspicious repo; demos |
| Full VM | Strongest | Full | Long-running work on untrusted code, kernel-level isolation |

Rule of thumb: **Docker or a VM for code you would not run directly; WSL for
convenience; Windows Sandbox for a single disposable session.**

## Docker

The server and every `shell_run` command execute **inside the container**.
The host is reachable only through what you mount.

```bash
# Workspace: read-write bind mount. Data + checkpoints: named volumes, never the
# host's real %LOCALAPPDATA%\venira (a bind mount would expose the host store).
docker run --rm -i \
  --network none \
  --read-only --tmpfs /tmp \
  -v /path/to/project:/workspace \
  -v venira-data:/data \
  -v venira-snapshots:/snapshots \
  -e VENIRA_WORKSPACE=/workspace \
  -e VENIRA_DATA_DIR=/data \
  -e VENIRA_SNAPSHOT_DIR=/snapshots/my-project \
  -e VENIRA_SECURITY_PROFILE=balanced \
  --user 1000:1000 \
  ghcr.io/your-org/venira-mcp:latest
```

MCP client config (stdio piped into the container):

```jsonc
{
  "mcp": {
    "venira": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": [
        "docker", "run", "--rm", "-i",
        "--network", "none",
        "-v", "C:\\src\\my-app:/workspace",
        "-v", "venira-data:/data",
        "-v", "venira-snapshots:/snapshots",
        "-e", "VENIRA_WORKSPACE=/workspace",
        "-e", "VENIRA_DATA_DIR=/data",
        "-e", "VENIRA_SNAPSHOT_DIR=/snapshots/my-app",
        "ghcr.io/your-org/venira-mcp:latest"
      ],
      "enabled": true
    }
  }
}
```

**Mounts**

- Mount only the project. Do not mount the repo root above it, the user profile,
  or the host data directory.
- Keep `VENIRA_DATA_DIR` and the checkpoint store on volumes owned by the container
  user. The data dir holds the audit chain, approval key and encrypted secrets.
- Never mount `/var/run/docker.sock`: it is root-equivalent on the host and defeats
  the boundary.
- `--read-only` with a writable `VENIRA_DATA_DIR` is a useful hardening default;
  the workspace bind mount stays writable where the agent must edit.

**Network**

- `--network none` is the strongest option. Everything still works except
  `shell_run` commands that need the network, git fetch/push, package
  installs, and the Git provider/CI tools.
- To keep provider/CI tools working, use a user-defined network with egress
  filtering, or an allowlist proxy. Do not use `--network host`.
- A container with network access can still exfiltrate the workspace. Treat
  "network on" as a deliberate trust decision.

**Limits**

- Shell commands run inside the container, so host binaries and host credentials
  are unavailable — unless you mounted them. `VENIRA_DEFAULT_SHELL` must name a
  shell that exists in the image.
- The image runs as root by default. Use `--user 1000:1000` and make the mounted
  volumes writable by that UID, or the audit DB and checkpoints fail to write.
- The MCP client itself runs on the host and owns the stdio pipe; the client's own
  file tools and extensions are outside this boundary.
- Docker Desktop on Windows/macOS adds a VM layer, but bind mounts still expose
  the mounted folder with the host user's permissions.
- Approvals need a human with a TTY. In a headless container, either use
  `VENIRA_SHELL_MODE=balanced` (ask-rule commands prompt through an elicitation-capable client),
  `strict`/`permissive` for the CLI grant path, or grant approvals from a terminal that can see
  the same data dir.

## WSL 2

Run the server **inside the distro** and keep the workspace on the Linux filesystem.

```bash
# Inside WSL
npm --prefix /home/me/venira-mcp install
VENIRA_WORKSPACE=/home/me/src/my-app \
VENIRA_DATA_DIR=/home/me/.local/share/venira \
VENIRA_SNAPSHOT_ROOT=/home/me/.local/share/venira/snapshots \
  node /home/me/venira-mcp/dist/server.js
```

MCP client config on Windows:

```jsonc
{
  "mcp": {
    "venira": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["wsl", "-d", "Ubuntu", "--", "node", "/home/me/venira-mcp/dist/server.js"],
      "environment": {
        "VENIRA_WORKSPACE": "/home/me/src/my-app",
        "VENIRA_DATA_DIR": "/home/me/.local/share/venira"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**Mounts and paths**

- Keep the project under `/home/...` (ext4). `/mnt/c/...` is slow, case-insensitive
  and reports Windows permissions; file mtimes and the workspace lock behave
  better on the native filesystem.
- `VENIRA_WORKSPACE` and the data/snapshot paths must be Linux paths. Windows paths
  are not translated.
- Shell commands run in the distro; `bash`/`sh` are available, PowerShell is not
  (unless you installed it inside WSL).

**Interop and network**

WSL 2 is **not** a security boundary against Windows: by default a process can run
`/mnt/c/Windows/System32/cmd.exe` and reach the whole `C:` drive. If you want some
separation, disable interop and Windows path injection in `/etc/wsl.conf`:

```ini
[interop]
enabled = false
appendWindowsPath = false
```

Then `wsl --shutdown`. This stops accidental host execution, but the same Windows
user can still read the distro's files and vice versa; it does not contain a
determined attacker.

WSL 2 shares the host network stack (NAT or mirrored mode). There is no
container-style `--network none`; restrict egress with Windows Firewall rules or
run Docker inside WSL when you need real network isolation. Set memory/CPU caps in
`%UserProfile%\.wslconfig` (`[wsl2] memory=8GB processors=4`) so a runaway build
cannot starve Windows.

**Limits**

- Same-user access from Windows via `\\wsl$\...`, and root inside the distro, are
  outside the guard.
- The data dir on ext4 is not encrypted unless the distro/disk is.
- A compromised Windows process can still start commands in the distro.

## Windows Sandbox

Windows Sandbox is a disposable VM. Use it to open a suspicious repository once,
with no lasting state on the host.

Requires Windows 10/11 **Pro, Enterprise or Education**, virtualization enabled in
firmware, and the "Windows Sandbox" optional feature installed.

`venira.wsb`:

```xml
<Configuration>
  <Networking>Disable</Networking>
  <MappedFolders>
    <MappedFolder>
      <HostFolder>C:\src\my-app</HostFolder>
      <SandboxFolder>C:\workspace</SandboxFolder>
      <ReadOnly>false</ReadOnly>
    </MappedFolder>
    <MappedFolder>
      <HostFolder>C:\src\venira-mcp</HostFolder>
      <SandboxFolder>C:\venira-mcp</SandboxFolder>
      <ReadOnly>true</ReadOnly>
    </MappedFolder>
  </MappedFolders>
  <LogonCommand>
    <Command>powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -NoProfile -Command "cd C:\venira-mcp; npm ci --omit=dev; node dist\server.js"</Command>
  </LogonCommand>
</Configuration>
```

Launch with `WindowsSandbox.exe C:\src\venira.wsb` (or double-click the file), then
point the MCP client at the sandbox process. Most clients cannot attach to a process
inside the sandbox; a practical pattern is to run the agent **inside** the sandbox
too, with the project mapped in.

**Mounts**

- Only mapped folders cross the boundary. The rest of the host is invisible.
- Map the project read-write only when the agent must edit it; prefer a copy.
- The sandbox's data dir and checkpoints are ephemeral. Map a separate writable
  folder if you need the audit trail or checkpoints after the session, and treat
  that folder as untrusted output.
- Mapped folders are shared with the host; a process in the sandbox can modify them
  with your host permissions.

**Network**

`<Networking>Disable</Networking>` removes network access entirely. Omit it (or use
`Enable`) when the toolchain needs package installs or the Git provider/CI tools;
then set up the image or a proxy beforehand. Windows Sandbox has no port-forwarding
configuration; use mapped folders for data exchange.

**Limits**

- Everything is destroyed when the sandbox closes: no audit history, no checkpoints,
  no installed packages.
- GPU, some USB devices and nested virtualization are unavailable by default.
- The host must run the sandbox; it is not a server deployment target.
- If you map a host folder read-write, a command can still damage that folder. Keep
  a backup or map a copy.
- Sandbox escape vulnerabilities exist; it is much stronger than nothing, not
  equivalent to a hardened VM with a separate kernel.

## Checklist before trusting a boundary

- [ ] Workspace is the only writable host path (or a copy).
- [ ] `VENIRA_DATA_DIR` and the checkpoint store are on container/VM storage, not
      the host profile.
- [ ] No Docker socket, home directory, SSH keys or cloud credential mounts.
- [ ] Network is `none` unless git/provider/CI/package installs are required.
- [ ] Shell commands execute inside the boundary (no host shell mounted).
- [ ] You can see and approve `ask` commands (TTY or elicitation).
- [ ] You know where the audit DB lives and how to read it after the session.

## Threat model (what this project does and does not defend against)

This MCP server runs with the privileges of the user that started it and
is designed for **trusted, local use** (your own machine, your own agent).
It is *not* a network-facing service. Understand the boundaries before
deploying:

### What is defended

- **Workspace path lock.** Every path is resolved against `VENIRA_WORKSPACE`
  (or `process.cwd()`). `../` and absolute paths that escape it are rejected
  with `path_escape`. This is a *first-line* guard, not a sandbox.
- **Cache correctness.** Read/info caches are validated by `mtime + size`,
  so an external edit or delete can never silently serve stale content.
- **Audit integrity.** Every operation is written to a SQLite WAL table with a
  keyed hash chain (`prev_hash`/`row_hash`, HMAC-SHA256 with `audit.key` in the
  data dir). `read_audit verify=1` recomputes the digest of the fields
  that are immutable after insert, so in-place edits or a rewritten chain fail
  verification unless the attacker also has the key file. Legacy databases with
  a required `created_at` column are supported in place; `health`
  surfaces orphan `running` rows as a post-mortem signal.
- **Secret store integrity.** Secret values are encrypted with AES-256-GCM and
  the secret name is bound in as AAD (swapping ciphertext between two names
  fails authentication). The metadata fingerprint is a keyed HMAC, not a plain
  SHA-256, so a leaked `secrets.json` cannot be brute-forced offline for
  low-entropy values. Read-modify-write operations run under a cross-process
  lock, so concurrent `set` calls cannot silently drop each other.
- **Native module supply chain.** `better-sqlite3` is the only native
  dependency; its build scripts are allowlisted via `npm approve-scripts`
  so an npm v12 install can't be tricked into running an unapproved script.

### What is NOT defended (by design, in scope of a local tool)

- **Prompt injection / malicious commands.** A malicious model output or a
  poisoned file it reads can still steer the agent to run a destructive
  shell command (`rm -rf`, `format`, …). The workspace lock bounds
  *filesystem* paths, not shell *side effects*. The audit log makes this
  visible *after* the fact.
- **Running the server as root / in a shared environment.** If the MCP
  client (OpenCode, etc.) runs the server in a context that can reach other
  users' data, the workspace lock does not isolate you from them.
- **A local attacker with access to `VENIRA_DATA_DIR`.** The audit chain and
  approval grants are HMAC-signed with keys kept in that directory. This stops
  DB-only or file-store-only tampering, but the same OS user (or root) can read
  the keys and re-sign anything. Use a separate account/container if that
  matters.
- **The MCP transport itself.** stdio transport is local; if you ever proxy
  it over a network, that layer's authn/z is out of scope for this project.

### Historical context

The broader MCP / agentic-coding ecosystem has seen several classes of
incident that are relevant here even though this project has not been
directly affected:

- **OpenCode "RCE flaw"** — an input-validation gap in an agentic coding
  harness that let a crafted workspace file steer the tool-execution
  pipeline into running attacker-chosen commands. The mitigation pattern:
  validate *and* log every tool argument at the boundary, and never trust
  content read from the workspace as a command. venira-mcp keeps
  tool arguments schema-checked (zod) and the audit table as the
  post-hoc record.
- **Agent / sandbox escape (e.g. "harness"-style escapes)** — agents that
  can write files or run shell can, in an over-permissive sandbox,
  escalate. Treat `shell_run` as the highest-risk tool. Choose
  `VENIRA_SECURITY_PROFILE=strict` or `balanced` for a more restrictive
  approval posture, or run the whole server in a container (see `DOCKER.md`).
- **npm supply-chain (install-time code execution)** — malicious or
  typosquatted dependencies running lifecycle scripts at install time.
  This is why the project pins its native dependency's script allowlist
  (`allowScripts`) and ships an `npm approve-scripts`-generated manifest.
  Renovate is configured to flag vulnerability advisories.

## Hardening checklist for operators

1. **Lock the workspace.** Leave `VENIRA_UNRESTRICTED` unset (or `0`).
   Only set it to `1` in a fully disposable environment.
2. **Contain the shell.** Choose `VENIRA_SECURITY_PROFILE=strict` for the
   read-only allowlist, or `balanced` to require approval for ask-rule and
   unclassified commands. Use a container when you need an OS-level boundary.
3. **Keep shell overrides off by default.** If one is necessary, enable only the named
   exception and review its per-call reason and `policy_rule` in the audit trail.
4. **Review the audit trail.** Periodically query `project_tool_audit`
   (or run `health` with `include_audit=1`) to confirm what the
   agent actually did.
5. **Least-privilege user.** Run the MCP client (and thus this server)
   as a regular user, not root.
6. **Update dependencies.** Renovate auto-opens PRs for vulnerability
   advisories; keep them green.
7. **Verify checksums** when using the release bundles
   (`.zip` / `.tgz` / Docker image) — SHA-256 values are published in
   every GitHub Release body.

## Approval model

Shell and JavaScript approval requests return a common `data.approval` payload, including the pending `approval_id`, the reviewed subject, expiry, approve command, and retry arguments. Only a human can grant by running the exact `data.approval.approve_command` from the response in an interactive PowerShell terminal or through MCP client elicitation; grants are HMAC-verified, bound to the exact call, expire after five minutes, and are single-use. Consumption is an atomic claim: if two retries race with the same id, exactly one runs. The pending record's displayed command/shell/cwd/secret_env must match the signed binding, so tampering with the record invalidates it. A `--session` grant is in-memory, lasts 10 minutes by default (`VENIRA_SHELL_APPROVAL_TTL_MS`), and is cleared by a server restart. The removed `approval_token` and `VENIRA_SHELL_AUTO_APPROVE_TOKEN` paths cannot approve a request; the legacy environment variable is ignored with a warning.

## Configuration posture

`health` (and `doctor`) report a shared `posture` object with a `level` (`ok` / `info` / `warning` / `critical`), deterministic findings carrying stable ids such as `workspace.unrestricted`, `profile.off`, `shell.mode_off`, `shell.mode_permissive`, `js.exec_without_approval`, `combo.unrestricted_open_shell`, `combo.unrestricted_unapproved_js`, `approval.session_grant_risky_rule`, `self_install.enabled`, `secret.reveal_enabled` and `git.plain_http_allowed`. Findings are warnings only (`fail_closed: false`): an invalid profile/mode/boolean already fails closed at startup, while the combinations above are valid operator choices. Making them refusals would break existing trusted/off deployments; revisit only with measured demand for an acknowledgement gate.

## Security-related environment variables

| Variable | Default | Security note |
|---|---|---|
| `VENIRA_UNRESTRICTED` | `"0"` | `"1"` removes the workspace lock. Highest-risk setting. |
| `VENIRA_SECURITY_PROFILE` | `balanced` | `strict` is most restrictive; `balanced` is recommended; `trusted` lets ask-rule and unclassified commands run and turns hard-deny into approval; `off` disables shell checks and per-call JS approval. |
| `VENIRA_SHELL_MODE` | Profile mapping | Advanced override: `strict`, `balanced`, `permissive`, or `off`. |
| `VENIRA_JS_EXEC_MODE` | `"off"` | `execute_js` gate: `off` hides it, `ask` per-call approval (contained), `semi-auto` no approval (contained: network blocked, workspace-only fs, scrubbed env), `auto` no approval and no containment. |
| `VENIRA_SHELL_OVERRIDES` | unset | Operator allowlist for specific named shell exceptions. Each tool call must pass the exact name and a reason; the reason is redacted and audited, but is not proof of human identity. |
| `VENIRA_DATA_DIR` | Per-user OS data directory | Contains the audit DB, encrypted secrets, approval key and pending approvals. Keep it private and don't point it at a shared directory. |
| `VENIRA_SESSION_GRANT_RULES` | `cd_outside_workspace` | Additional rules eligible for human-approved session grants. Do not include network or history-rewrite rules unless the environment is disposable. |
| `VENIRA_SHELL_APPROVAL_TTL_MS` | `600000` (10 min) | Lifetime of an in-memory `--session` grant. Pending approvals are always fixed at 5 minutes. |
| `VENIRA_SESSION_ID` | auto | Set it in tests so audit rows are separable. |

Boolean environment flags and boolean-like MCP tool arguments accept only numeric `0` or `1`. Invalid legacy spellings fail explicitly; provider workflow input booleans are data and are not changed.

# venira-mcp — Shell Security

Status: implementation complete for the v1.15.0 approval/profile work. Local validation last run 2026-11-06; see the commands and results below. Shell policy is a guard rail, not an OS sandbox.

## Security profiles

`VENIRA_SECURITY_PROFILE` selects the baseline. Unset means `balanced`; unknown values fail startup validation.

| Profile | Shell mode | JavaScript approval | Behavior |
|---|---|---|---|
| `strict` | `strict` | on | Safe workspace commands and the read-only allowlist run; other commands ask; hard-deny rules deny |
| `balanced` (default) | `balanced` | on | Routine safe commands run; ask rules and unclassified commands ask; hard-deny rules deny |
| `trusted` | `permissive` | on | Ask-rule and unclassified commands run; hard-deny commands ask for approval |
| `off` | `off` | off | Shell checks are bypassed with a startup warning and audit record; use only in a trusted environment |

`VENIRA_SHELL_MODE` is an advanced override. `VENIRA_JS_EXEC_MODE` (`off` / `ask` / `semi-auto` / `auto`) separately gates the JavaScript tool: it is not registered unless the mode is not `off`, `ask` needs per-call approval, `semi-auto` needs none but keeps the snippet contained, and `auto` needs none and removes the containment. The `secret_env` injection gate always requires approval, including in `off`.

## Approval lifecycle

All gated shell and JavaScript calls use the same approval core:

1. The server creates a pending `approval_id` bound to the exact command or code, shell, cwd, rule, and secret environment names.
2. A human grants it through the interactive `npx venira-mcp --approve <id>` CLI or client elicitation. The CLI requires a TTY.
3. The agent retries once with that `approval_id`. Grants are HMAC-verified, expire after five minutes, and are single-use.

There is no agent-redeemable `approval_token` or `VENIRA_SHELL_AUTO_APPROVE_TOKEN`; the legacy environment variable is warned about and ignored. Responses include a shared `data.approval` payload with a ready-to-use retry shape. `approval_wait_ms` can keep a call open for up to 45 seconds while the human grants it.

`shell_run.dry_run=1` reports the policy result without running the command or creating an approval. Hard-deny behavior is: `strict` and `balanced` deny; `trusted` asks; `off` bypasses shell policy. Deny always wins over ask rules except in the explicitly permissive `trusted` posture, where a hard-deny match requires a grant.
